title: Quebec premier slams Kinew's description of secularism law as 'legislative racism'

image.caption: Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew made the comment when he was asked, during a news conference on Friday, to react to the Supreme Court decision regarding the fate of Quebec's secularism law, known as Bill 21. (Gilbert Rowan/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is asking that Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew retract his comments characterizing Quebec's secularism law as "legislative racism."
Kinew made the comment while reacting to Friday's Supreme Court decision

On Friday, the Supreme Court upheld Quebec's use of the notwithstanding clause when the province passed Bill 21 in 2019. The law forbids certain public sector workers from wearing religious symbols at work.
When asked to react to the ruling at a news conference Friday, Kinew said the law was "designed to discriminate against Muslims primarily, but also Sikhs and other religious minorities."
He also said the law would be deemed discriminatory were it not for the notwithstanding clause, which shields it from court challenges.

items: Upheld Quebec religious symbols bill 'legislative racism,' Manitoba premier says

blocks.text: On Saturday, St-Pierre Plamondon took to social media to "strongly denounce" Kinew's comments.

"Not only has the Supreme Court confirmed the validity of Quebec’s secularism, but it has also affirmed the legitimacy of our distinct approach to this issue," St-Pierre Plamondon wrote in French in a post to X.

items: Canada's top court upholds Quebec law banning some workers from wearing religious symbols

blocks.text: Manitoba, along with B.C., intervened in the Quebec case to argue that courts should be able to rule on whether laws protected by the notwithstanding clause violate sections of the Charter.
The Supreme Court justices ruled in their favour on that point.
The two leaders are set to attend the premiers meeting on Dec. 7 in Toronto.
